articles.title: Democrats rake in cash, Musk takes center stage for GOP: 5 takeaways from latest fundraising hauls
articles.summary: Democrats running in competitive Senate races are raking in cash as they race to close the financial gap with Republicans, who have been buoyed in part by Elon Musk and his super PAC. Democrat James Talarico’s campaign for Texas Senate alone raised a staggering $60 million between July, August and September, while Sen. Jon Ossoff…
articles.body:
Democrats running in competitive Senate races are raking in cash as they race to close the financial gap with Republicans , who have been buoyed in part by Elon Musk and his super PAC.

Democrat James Talarico’s campaign for Texas Senate alone raised a staggering $60 million between July, August and September, while Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) brought in $33 million and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed raked in close to $31 million in the Michigan Senate contest —dwarfing their GOP counterparts.

But Musk, the tech billionaire and former Trump adviser, has served as a bright spot for Republicans, with his super PAC effectively bankrolling Texas Senate GOP candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign.

This investment has made the fierce contest one of the most expensive Senate races in history — with more than $500 million spent or reserved in advertising in total between the two parties, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact . The firm is also forecasting that the 2026 election could be the most expensive midterm cycle ever .

Here are five takeaways from the last quarterly filing before Election Day:

Democrats post blockbuster numbers in Senate races

It’s not just Talarico, Ossoff and El-Sayed who are outraising their Republican counterparts in key races.

Battleground Senate Democratic candidates have outraised their opponents: former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown’s campaign raised $23 million , Maine’s Troy Jackson collected more than $20 million , former Rep. Mary Peltola (Alaska) posted $14 million , and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper’s campaign raked in $12.2 million .

Meanwhile, Paxton’s campaign raised more than $10 million ; Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, a former House lawmaker, posted $9.7 million ; Sen. Jon Husted (R) raised close to $5 million in Ohio ; Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) reported $5.2 million ; Georgia’s Republican candidate Rep. Mike Collins posted $2.8 million ; former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, who is running against Cooper, reported $2.1 million ; and Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R) campaign raised $2 million in Alaska.

Adam Hamilton, a pastor running as a Democrat for Senate in Kansas, even raised more than Sen. Roger Marshall (R). The Democrat’s campaign brought in more than $9 million while Marshall’s campaign reported just more than $800,000 .

That doesn’t mean Republicans aren’t making those numbers up elsewhere — those figures don’t account for joint fundraising accounts, super PAC spending to benefit or oppose candidates, or their general financial advantage at the party level.

Still, the higher campaign fundraising gives Democrats more bang for their buck with ad buys. Senate Democratic candidates also outraised their GOP peers last quarter.

Musk dives back into political fray to boost GOP

Musk and his super PAC, America PAC, have become key assets for Republicans this cycle as the GOP looks to keep parity with Democrats on fundraising. Musk donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) PAC, which is associated with Senate GOP leadership.

The contributions, $75 million and $83 million, were each made to the super PAC. A day after SLF PAC received those contributions, they were immediately transferred to Texas PAC , which is a Senate GOP leadership-aligned group backing Paxton.

Texas PAC’s quarterly report shows that Musk financed the group entirely.

America PAC has also been very active this cycle, spending more than $76 million this quarter in various battleground Senate and House races. These include contests for Senate in Michigan, Texas and Alaska as well as House races in battlegrounds such as Arizona’s 1st District and New York’s 17th District.

Wintour, Bush, Blinken among big names donating

Musk isn’t the only big name spending big in the lead-up to the election.

Anna Wintour, Condé Nast’s chief content officer and global editorial director of Vogue, donated $5,000 to Talarico’s joint fundraising committee. Several members of the Soros family — Robert, Catherine and Jamie — gave a combined $15,000 to the same group.

Stephen Jones, co-owner and CEO of the Dallas Cowboys, gave $122,000 to Paxton’s joint fundraising committee , Paxton Victory, while the group received a separate $100,000 from Jerry Jones, the franchise’s president and owner. Major Texas GOP donor Farris Wilks gave $250,000 to his joint fundraising committee in addition to Texas businessman Alex Fairly, who gave more than $270,000.

Four top SpaceX employees also gave more than $33,000 combined to another joint fundraising committee for Paxton, Team Paxton.

Former President George W. Bush gave Collins $3,500 for her campaign , and longtime GOP strategist Karl Rove gave her campaign $1,500 . Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken gave $1,750 to Ossoff’s campaign. Seven Anthropic employees gave more than $24,000 combined to Ossoff as well.

While some super PACs and other political groups have not yet filed — groups that report monthly will file later this month while those that file biyearly will only file again next January — the 2026 spending picture is coming into focus.

Anthropic’s political action committee spent more than $250,000 between July and September, including $161,000 last month alone, according to figures first shared with The Hill. The group had a nearly even spending split between Republicans and Democrats.

The political group gave money to the campaign arms for Senate Republicans and Democrats in addition to a handful of senators and House members on both sides.

More recently, Think Big and American Mission , both super PACs aligned with the pro-AI Leading the Future group, have spent money in a handful of House races.

Meanwhile, United Democracy Project, the super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, has so far spent shy of $190,000 opposing El-Sayed in the general election.

MAHA PAC wades into Iowa governor’s race

Allies of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement are investing in the Iowa gubernatorial race to support Republican Zach Lahn. MAHA PAC and MAHA Action PAC announced Thursday that they would be spending more than $1.65 million to support Lahn as he battles against Democrat Rob Sand for the Iowa governor’s seat.

MAHA PAC is spending $150,000 of that money on get-out-the-vote field operations, while $1.5 million is being donated directly to Lahn’s campaign by MAHA Action PAC. MAHA PAC endorsed the candidate last year.

MAHA PAC is investing in half a dozen House races, too.

Statewide races typically follow different campaign finance reporting deadlines as they vary from state to state.

Lahn has leaned into issues aligned with the MAHA movement, particularly his focus on tackling cancer, as the Hawkeye State has one of the highest rates of new cancer in the U.S.

articles.title: Three things we learned from the US midterm debates
articles.summary: As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged.
articles.body:
Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.

As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.

1. Not all Republicans are standing behind Trump

Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?

Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.

The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.

Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.

"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.

"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.

Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.

In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.

She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.

Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.

During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.

The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."

As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.

The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.

Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.

He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".

On Thursday, as a protester interrupted a Maine debate between Jackson and Collins, who suggested that the person interrupting the debate was associated with her opponent.

Jackson then said to Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."

Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.

What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".

Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.

In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".

Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".

"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.

3. Some candidates are skipping debates entirely

There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.

One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.

Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

articles.title: Biden judge rejects Obama CIA chief's legal bid against Trump over one key problem
articles.summary: John Brennan's lawsuit against Trump and senior officials was dismissed, but grand jury investigations into the former CIA director continue.
articles.body: A Biden-appointed judge dismissed former CIA Director John Brennan's lawsuit against President Donald Trump and senior administration officials, ruling that his concerns about the potential destruction of evidence needed for a future criminal defense were too "speculative." The dismissal comes as Brennan faces two federal investigations, including a Justice Department probe into whether former intelligence officials conspired to violate Trump's civil rights through investigations into alleged ties between his 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. A separate investigation is examining whether Brennan made false statements during 2023 congressional testimony about the Steele dossier's role in a 2017 intelligence assessment of Russian interference in the presidential election. FORMER CIA DIRECTOR BRENNAN SUBPOENAED TO TESTIFY IN FEDERAL TRUMP CONSPIRACY CASE Trump has repeatedly accused Brennan, President Barack Obama and other former intelligence officials of orchestrating the "Russia collusion hoax," but they have rejected those accusations, claiming that the administration is attempting to discredit legitimate intelligence findings about Russian interference in the 2016 election. While Judge Jia Cobb called Brennan’s allegations that the Trump administration was targeting him for opposing the president "deeply concerning," she ruled that he lacked standing to sue because he had not shown that officials were likely destroying records relevant to a potential defense, and the injury he feared depended on a series of events that had not yet occurred. "For Brennan’s constitutional injury to actually accrue, a series of dominoes must fall, and Defendants’ deletion of records is just one of those dominoes," Cobb wrote. "There is no dispute about this: Defendants describe this domino chain in their motion to dismiss ... and Brennan accepts it in his response." Brennan has been identified as a target in two federal investigations that have involved three grand jury inquiries — two in the Southern District of Florida and one in Washington, D.C. — but he has not been charged with a crime. The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, Oct. 15, though his scheduled appearance was postponed. Brennan filed his lawsuit naming Trump, FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and other officials July 1, 2026. The 46-page lawsuit accused the Justice Department of handling its investigation into Brennan with "unprecedented, irregular conduct" that was driven by the "president’s retribution agenda." DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’ Brennan argued that key evidence could disappear before he had a chance to challenge any future indictment. He pointed to deleted social media posts, the administration’s use of Signal and other messaging tools with auto-delete features, unpreserved texts and direct messages, AI queries, Microsoft Teams chats and alleged failures to preserve discovery in other cases, including the prosecution of Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J. He said the loss of those records could make it harder to determine whether the investigations were based on legitimate law enforcement concerns or political retaliation. "With this lawsuit, Director Brennan has served notice that the government’s conduct and its document preservation will be carefully scrutinized in the event of any future indictment," Brennan’s lawyers, Ken Wainstein and Dan Gelber, told the AP. "Director Brennan will continue to vigorously defend himself against these baseless investigations, and he will challenge any attempt to use the criminal justice system for personal and political retribution." The lawsuit also pointed to what it described as irregularities in the Justice Department’s handling of the investigation. It cited the removal of longtime DOJ prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who was reportedly taken off the Brennan investigation in April 2026 after expressing doubts about the strength of the case, as evidence of what it described as irregular conduct. She was replaced by Trump ally Joseph diGenova, who later resigned from his role overseeing the investigation amid reported internal disagreements over the handling of the case. TRUMP SAYS HE WILL NOMINATE ACTING AG TODD BLANCHE TO PERMANENTLY LEAD JUSTICE DEPARTMENT Brennan’s attorneys accused the Justice Department of "judge-shopping" by trying to steer grand jury proceedings toward Trump-appointed Judge Aileen Cannon in Fort Pierce, Florida, rather than allowing the case to proceed through the court's normal assignment process. They also questioned why prosecutors were pursuing the investigation in Florida when much of the allegations occurred in Washington, D.C. The complaint also accused DOJ and FBI leaders of improperly discussing details of the investigations publicly, raising questions about whether officials disclosed information that should have remained confidential. It cited Attorney General Todd Blanche’s statements that DOJ had issued "200 grand jury subpoenas" and was investigating a "pattern of behavior" to "destroy" Trump, as well as FBI Director Kash Patel’s public discussion of the investigations and their targets. articles.title: Mamdani, New York Democrats call on private parking lot owners to ban ICE officers
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and other Empire State Democratic leaders urged the city’s private parking lot owners Friday to ban Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from their properties. “In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent,…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and other Empire State Democratic leaders urged the city’s private parking lot owners Friday to ban Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from their properties.

“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the mayor wrote in a letter to owners and operators of these properties.

More than 100 elected officials, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), signed on to Mamdani’s request.

The New York Democrats cited the recent ICE-involved shooting of Oscar Belgal in the city’s Marble Hill neighborhood last week while his 5-year-old son was in the car with him.

Following the shooting, the mayor condemned the Oct. 8 shooting as “unconscionable” in a social media post and demanded that all ICE enforcement operations be halted in the city.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said Belgal was an immigrant who had a prior criminal conviction and arrests.

The Friday letter pointed out that the federal immigration officials involved in the incident utilized a privately owned parking lot during their operations.

“Federal agents are turning to private parking lots, including a lot just blocks from where they shot Mr. Belgal,” Mamdani said in a Friday statement . “I am asking every garage and lot owner in this city to stop giving them that option. Do not rent your property to ICE. Do not lend it to them. Tell them they are not welcome.”

The Democratic officials pointed to an executive order the mayor signed earlier this year barring external law enforcement agencies, such as ICE, from staging operations on city property unless they have a judicial warrant or meet other “limited legal exceptions.”

“Time and again, New York City has made it through challenging moments because government, business and community leaders come together and show the world what New Yorkers can do,” the Democratic officials wrote in their Friday letter. “Owners who refuse to take part in these federal civil immigration enforcement operations advance public safety by protecting their own staff and customers, as well as fellow New Yorkers beyond their lots and garages. “

“They also tell every immigrant New Yorker that they are treasured members of this community and that our City welcomes them with open arms,” they continued. “We hope you will stand with us.”

A DHS spokesperson told The Hill on Friday that barring federal agents from parking lots would not halt deportation operations in the city.

“Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t,” the DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again.”

articles.title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
articles.summary: Speed curbs limited Ukraine's defences against deadly Russian attacks on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.

"It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored.

Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.

Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.

Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon.

The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.

Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.

Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks.

"If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.

Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".

But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.

Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".

Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.

In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.

The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.

On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.

Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.

A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network.

"Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.

On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.

Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine.

Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.

The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.

Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.

articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) made a $1 million donation to Abdul El-Sayed’s (D) Michigan Senate campaign, a campaign spokesperson confirmed to The Hill on Friday. El-Sayed is locked in a tight contest for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat, facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). Ocasio-Cortez said she made the donation because she did not…
articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) made a $1 million donation to Abdul El-Sayed’s (D) Michigan Senate campaign, a campaign spokesperson confirmed to The Hill on Friday.

El-Sayed is locked in a tight contest for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat, facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). Ocasio-Cortez said she made the donation because she did not want to regret not doing more for El-Sayed if he loses.

“I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement to The Hill. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 68 percent chance of winning the Michigan Senate race.

The New York congresswoman said she made the donation using campaign funds from more than 2 million donors, not from her personal wealth.

“It is not MY contribution. It is OUR contribution,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a fundraising email.

Ocasio-Cortez is crisscrossing the nation ahead of the midterms, rallying with other progressives including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign tour for El-Sayed has included multiple stops across Michigan this week.

This cycle, Ocasio-Cortez has been more selective with her endorsements. She endorsed in only a handful of the congressional Democratic primary fights . She chose to endorse El-Sayed in his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), whom he defeated narrowly. She also endorsed a slate of progressive candidates in the New York state legislative primaries.

Her endorsements and rallies have increased speculation that she may choose to run for president in 2028. While she has not yet made up her mind on the decision, she told The New York Times last month that she may only get one chance.

“Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

articles.title: Trump claims neither he nor Musk caused Ukraine Starlink outage
articles.summary: President Trump claimed on Friday that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk caused Ukraine’s Starlink outage earlier this week as the president clashed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries. “I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was…
articles.body:
President Trump claimed on Friday that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk caused Ukraine’s Starlink outage earlier this week as the president clashed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries.

“I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning,” Trump told reporters Friday while on his way to a campaign rally in Georgia.

“I heard about it from the news, the media. And we didn’t slow it down at all. And I think it’s probably functioning, from what I understand,” he continued.

When asked by a reporter if Musk was involved, Trump said, “I don’t know if there’s anybody because it wasn’t me, and it wasn’t Elon, as I understand.”

A White House official similarly told NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner, that “no such request” was ever made by Trump.

The outage was reported by Ukraine on Wednesday, saying that its military lost access to the military version of Starlink, which it uses for vital communications.

Starlink services were cut off specifically for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

At the time, some Ukrainian officials speculated the decision to restrict its access may have come from Washington.

Musk initially deferred to Trump, saying on the social platform X , “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company,” Musk wrote.

The conflict over access to Starlink marked a flash point in relations between Zelensky and Trump as he said the Ukrainian president was “ not a good guy for us to deal with .”

Multiple GOP senators expressed concern earlier this week that loss of access to critical Starlink servers had “degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure.”

“Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation,” the group of GOP senators wrote in a letter to Platte Moring, the Pentagon’s inspector general.

articles.title: Voto Latino reveals 6-figure Texas investment alongside Talarico, Hinojosa event
articles.summary: Voto Latino on Friday unveiled a new six-figure investment aimed at boosting Latino voter engagement in Texas with early voting kicking off in the state next week. The civic engagement organization said in a news release first shared with The Hill that it was investing more than $500,000 in the state. The investment comes ahead…
articles.body:
Voto Latino on Friday unveiled a new six-figure investment aimed at boosting Latino voter engagement in Texas with early voting kicking off in the state next week.

The civic engagement organization said in a news release first shared with The Hill that it was investing more than $500,000 in the state. The investment comes ahead of the group’s event in the Rio Grande Valley later this month with Democratic candidates running in closely watched midterm races.

President Trump and Republicans have seen his support among Latino voters slip heading into the November elections, in which he has repeatedly urged Americans to cast their votes as if he were “on the ballot.” This voting demographic was key to the president’s 2024 victory in the state.

Maria Teresa Kumar, the group’s president and co-founder, called Texas “ground zero for change” in a statement announcing the investment.

“We are heading straight to the epicenter of the Latino vote to make sure every voter is ready to cast their ballot,” Kumar said. “Latinos are on the brink of changing the political landscape of Texas and the nation.”

The group’s Oct. 25 event will feature three Democratic candidates in tightly contested midterm races, including gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, Senate hopeful James Talarico and House candidate Bobby Pulido.

Hinojosa, who is running to unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), said there was “no better place” to close out her campaign.

“For too long, Texans have been paying more and getting less under Greg Abbott,” she said in a statement. “I’m proud to be joining Voto Latino, making sure every family in the Valley has the information and the power to make their voice heard from now until Election Day.”

Talarico is running in a tightly contested race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

“Latino families in Texas have always carried this state forward, and they should have leaders who listen and deliver,” he said in a statement. “Our democracy works best when every neighbor has a seat at the table, and I’m grateful to Voto Latino for bringing us together for these final days.”

Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning singer from the Rio Grande Valley, is running in the state’s 15th District against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz.

“What I hear from families isn’t about left or right. They want good jobs, affordable health care, and schools that give their kids a real shot,” he said in a statement. “Our community has always shown up for one another, and I’m proud to be here with Voto Latino to make sure every voice in the Valley is heard.”

articles.title: AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push
articles.summary: Progressive stalwart, who is seen as potential 2028 candidate, says she wants to combat ‘smears’ against El-Sayed.
articles.body:
United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1m to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in a major progressive push for the upstart politician.

Ocasio-Cortez, who has become a progressive stalwart since her surprise 2018 congressional victory, confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and a speech in Michigan. The transfer was first reported by the New York Times.

The lawmaker pointed to political attacks against El-Sayed, a large portion of which have focused on his Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine.

“I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement, in reference to the November 3 congressional midterm election. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.”

Speaking at an event in the Detroit area, Ocasio added that she transferred the money from her own campaign to show “the cavalry is coming”.

“And the only reason I’m doing that is because I see the energy of each and every one of you stepping up to make an effort,” she said.

The move comes as Ocasio-Cortez has been campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, joining him on a bus tour of the conservative-leaning Upper Peninsula area before hosting three events on Friday in the state’s largest city, Detroit.

El Sayed’s populist progressive message has gained traction with voters in the state, where he currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls.

The support from Ocasio Cortez, who is weighing a potential 2028 presidential candidacy, also underscores a wider effort by progressives to court disaffected Trump voters. The pair highlighted economic issues while on the trail in the midwestern state.

Trump’s approval ratings are at a career low ahead of the midterm vote. A slate of recent polls has shown widespread public disapproval of Trump’s handling of the US economy and the knock-on effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Recent polls have also shown an appetite for a more comprehensive change in US government, signalling a potential opening for candidates running outside of the establishment of both major parties.

An AP-NORC poll released this week found that 80 percent of respondents said they supported either a “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how the country is run.

Speaking alongside Ocasio-Cortez on Friday, progressive House Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which raises and allocates funds for Senate candidates, to make “an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates” like El-Sayed, Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom.

El-Sayed, who received an early endorsement from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has also recently been embraced by a handful of more centrist Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Sanders donated $250,000 to El-Sayed’s campaign, CNN reports.

The new financial support from Ocasio-Cortez, which was given to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, arrived as the Michigan Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the state’s history, topping $268m as of October 15, according to the Detroit Free Press.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, outpaced Rogers in fundraising from July 1 to September 30, bringing in $30.6m compared to Rogers’ $9.6m. Still, Rogers’ campaign had more cash on hand as of September 30, with $6.5m compared to El-Sayed’s $3.8 million.

Michigan is among the key Senate races that could determine control of the chamber for the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term.

Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member body.

articles.title: Obama's star power gets a reality check from Black voters in crucial Senate race: 'It's a turnoff'
articles.summary: Barack Obama's endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed drew mixed reactions from Black Detroit voters, with undecided residents saying it didn't move the needle.
articles.body: DETROIT — Former President Barack Obama’s endorsement of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is getting a mixed reception among Black voters in Detroit, with some undecided voters saying the former president's backing isn't enough to win them over. Fox News Digital spoke with more than a dozen Black voters in Detroit, most of whom said they plan to back El-Sayed in November, but several undecided voters said Obama's endorsement had not persuaded them to support the Democrat. The reactions come as Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers seeks to win over disaffected Democrats, including Black voters in Detroit, a key constituency for the party in Michigan. "Honestly, it's a turn-off just because I've seen too many candidates use him just to manipulate the Democratic vote," Mercedes, one undecided Black voter, told Fox News Digital of Obama's endorsement. BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’ "No, not at all," Anthony, another undecided Black voter, told Fox News Digital when asked if Obama’s endorsement had swayed him toward El-Sayed. "What he's been able to do is from an image standpoint, as far as ‘hope,’ he drove the point there. But as far as really giving back to the community, minority owned businesses, and everyone across the board, I don't really think he really got there for me … he really hasn't swayed me one way or another." Obama and El-Sayed are preparing to campaign together in Michigan despite the Democratic Senate nominee's history of sharply criticizing the former president, a political reversal that also drew mixed reactions from Black Detroit voters interviewed by Fox News Digital. Juanita, another Black voter who has yet to commit to El-Sayed, told Fox News Digital that, "I don't want to be pushed to vote for him because somebody else is backing him." Rita, a Black voter who said she had recently been homeless, told Fox News Digital that she would prefer to do her own research rather than relying on Obama’s endorsement. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES Even some voters who support El-Sayed stated that Obama’s endorsement didn’t do much for them. "I think that a lot of people put more stock into who the person is than what he does … his yay or nay doesn't sway me either way," one such voter told Fox News Digital. Detroit’s African American residents were not uniform in dismissing Obama’s endorsement, however. Roughly half of those who spoke with Fox News Digital said the former president’s backing improved their opinion of El-Sayed, though none of those voters claimed that they were undecided before the endorsement. "For sure, I’m an Obama stan," Jamel, a Black voter planning to support El-Sayed, told Fox News Digital when asked whether Obama’s endorsement made him more likely to back the Democrat. "Somebody who is endorsed by Obama, I would want to vote for them, because I stand behind the things he endorsed at the time, and I think that Obama’s endorsement means a lot to our community," Kenya, another Black voter, told Fox News Digital. Detroit's Black voters were also divided over El-Sayed’s past criticism of Obama, particularly now that the two are preparing to campaign together. ‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE In a 2012 opinion column, El-Sayed accused then-President Obama of perpetuating war, violating civil liberties and deporting more people than any previous president. He described Obama’s reelection as "no victory," writing, "it was the rock we chose over the hard place." El-Sayed has since walked back those criticisms, praising Obama’s handling of the circumstances he inherited and noting that it is possible to disagree with someone while still admiring them. "Yeah, I don't understand how you can endorse somebody that was kind of the opposition when you were in office," Juanita told Fox News Digital. "I mean, that doesn't make sense." "I think I see it as a flip flop, but I also see it as an opportunity to pretty much highlight those things and how he's actually changed and why their objectives may align now," Anthony said. "You know, people's objectives change, their perspectives change." Nia, an African American voter who said she intends to support El-Sayed, said that pivots like El-Sayed’s are common in politics, pointing to Vice President JD Vance’s past criticism of President Donald Trump as an example. Despite mixed reactions to Obama's endorsement and El-Sayed's past criticism, several Black voters interviewed by Fox News Digital acknowledged the former president's continuing influence within the Democratic Party. HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL "He is. I mean, you can't deny that he has a gigantic following and a lot of people will follow him and will listen to what he has to say," Vincent, a Black voter who voted early for El-Sayed, told Fox News Digital. "But we're coming into a point in time now where we want to see results on both sides. We're not seeing results from either party, so we have to see results. So he may still have a big sway in the party now, but I think party politics is coming to an end kind of quick." While Fox News Digital's interviews were limited in number, they echo concerns about El-Sayed's support among Black voters that have surfaced in other reporting and polling. Pre-primary polling showed stronger support for Rep. Haley Stevens among Black Democratic voters, and questions have persisted about whether El-Sayed can consolidate that support heading into November. A recent focus group of Black voters held by MS NOW, for instance, found reluctance among Black Michigan voters to cast their lot with El-Sayed. A Fox News poll conducted in late September found that just 77% of African American voters were supportive of El-Sayed, significantly below the usual Democratic benchmark for the demographic. "I think he’s taking advantage [of] we as Black people are Democratic, and he think we gonna vote for him anyway," one middle-aged Black woman told the MS NOW panel. "And I’m like, ‘No sir, I’m gonna put uncommitted down on that little circle and move on.’ If you’re going to Congress to represent me, I need you to talk about what’s going on in this community." While the GOP sees an opportunity here, the party has long attempted to court minority support, with mixed results. Kandia Milton, a government affairs professional with deep ties to Detroit's African American community, pushed back against the narrative that El-Sayed would struggle with Black voters in November. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS BACKS EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY DEFEAT, CALLS SOCIALISM ‘DANGEROUS’ "The great thing about Abdul is that he's not new to Detroiters. … And so Detroiters, once they understand his background, understand what he stands for and all the things that he's done in the past, you see greater enthusiasm for his campaign and his candidacy for Senate," Milton said of El-Sayed. "He has been very active in getting out into the community. In fact, tomorrow we have a public meeting with Abdul at our church. Where he will be speaking to the community around, you know, the issues that he stands on and stands firm on." Milton characterized Obama's endorsement of El-Sayed as a "great shot in the arm" for his campaign, citing the former president's "credibility in our community" and arguing that the endorsement "puts to rest this notion that there's some tension between him and former President Obama." Milton wasn't surprised, however, that some Black voters said Obama's endorsement alone wasn't enough to win their support. "I think so often we take for granted the fact that many of the voters are informed voters, all of them are informed voters, and so it's not just the fact that Obama supported him, thus I'm going to vote for Abdul. A lot of folks are doing their own research," Milton told Fox News Digital. "They're very curious about Abdul. They see a lot of him on social media, in the media, national media as well. And so it has raised eyebrows and a lot of curiosity around who this guy is." Obama’s endorsement comes as both sides are trying to eke out every possible advantage they can in what is likely to be a very tight race. Fox News’ most recent Power Rankings has Michigan’s Senate race categorized as a "toss-up," meaning that neither party has an edge. articles.title: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary after 5 days on the job: reports
articles.summary: Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had already "fired" Zacharia.
articles.body:
President Trump signaled on Friday that he might replace embattled new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after less than one week on the job.

Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports.

If confirmed, that would make Zacharia the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history.

"We're talking about doing something," Trump told reporters outside the White House, adding that he told Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this."

"I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said.

Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media."

Trump said he would discuss the matter further with Zacharia when he returns from a Friday campaign rally in Georgia.

The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August.

Zacharia started at the White House on Monday gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda.

In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State.

In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer.

But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia."

Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China."

In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question."

Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job.

In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time.

On Thursday, Zacharia confimed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China."

On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer."

White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome."

Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added.

Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law."

"I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'"

On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation .

"Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?"

"When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law."

What happened in Zacharia's first briefing?

Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement.

"I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time."

She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing.

Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people."

In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning."

Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X .

The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile .

She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol."

Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children.

During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary.

"The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here."

Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon.

CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position."

In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class.

"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent."

articles.title: Rep. Andy Harris on spat with student reporter: ‘I pushed back, liberal media got offended’
articles.summary: Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) is defending himself after video of him clashing with a student reporter during a press gaggle went viral earlier this week. In an appearance on Fox 45 Baltimore Thursday, anchor Mikenzie Frost asked Harris about the moment and pressed him on if he regretted the exchange. “It’s not very newsworthy that…
articles.body:
Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) is defending himself after video of him clashing with a student reporter during a press gaggle went viral earlier this week.

In an appearance on Fox 45 Baltimore Thursday, anchor Mikenzie Frost asked Harris about the moment and pressed him on if he regretted the exchange.

“It’s not very newsworthy that the liberal media badgers a conservative politician, what was newsworthy is that I actually pushed back against it,” Harris said. “She actually started by criticizing the way that press gaggle was being conducted. That’s not the role of a journalist.”

The video , which the Baltimore Banner posted to social platform X Wednesday, shows Harris asking Capital News Service reporter Cat Murphy to stop recording the press gaggle, claiming she needed permission to do so under Maryland’s two-party consent law before appearing to threaten her with legal action.

However, the law Harris cited does not apply to public situations with “no reasonable expectation of privacy.”

Another video angle , shared by the Baltimore Sun on X, shows Murphy telling Harris to “respect their questions just as much as mine,” though it is not clear in the video what prompted the comment. Harris responded by saying he would not answer her questions.

Harris appeared to reference this moment during his Thursday interview, telling Frost that the reporter had been “telling me how to conduct the press conference” — which he also said is not the “purpose” of a journalist in this setting.

In an appearance on CNN, Murphy told anchor Jake Tapper the incident has been “a lot” to take in.

“It has been a lot. But I was focused on doing my job and asking my questions that I wanted answers to, and I think I did that,” Murphy said.

In Harris’ Fox 45 interview, Frost pointed out that Harris threatened to bring in police and have Murphy prosecuted for recording him, prompting the GOP lawmaker to reiterate his argument that Murphy was violating the two-party consent law during the interaction.

Harris went on to repeatedly blame “the liberal media” for the incident and subsequent social media firestorm. The GOP lawmaker is the current chair and an original member of the House Freedom Caucus, which includes some of the most conservative members of Congress.

“The liberal media has been doing this for years. Nobody pushes back. I pushed back, liberal media got offended,” Harris said.

The gaggle in question occurred after Harris wrapped up a debate against his opponent, Democrat Dan Schwartz, in the race for Maryland’s 1st Congressional District. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Harris, the incumbent, a 95 percent chance of victory in November.

articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said Friday it is restricting unauthorized drones along the ​U.S.-Mexico border.

This move comes as the government ramps up efforts to address concerns about illegal drug shipment across the border, Reuters reported Friday .

It is a temporary flight restriction that bars any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet above ground and extends 1 nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border, the report said.

In February, the FAA temporarily closed the airspace over El Paso, Texas, and southern New Mexico as a result of the Pentagon’s plan to test antidrone technology . The order was lifted hours later.

Later in August, the U.S. military used a high-energy laser to shoot down three drones near the southern border that officials said were linked to Mexican drug cartels . This operation involved the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to bring down the drones along the U.S.-Mexican border.

Customs and Boder Protection sources said the following month that the number of suspected cartel-linked drones in the Rio Grande Valley region of Texas along the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped by 75 percent since the military started using the high-energy lasers.

Officials, however, acknowledged that the drop in the number could be due to the cartel changing routes or using other tactics to achieve the goal of surveilling U.S. activity.

The FAA’s drone sighting report says the administration receives more than 100 reports of sightings each month from law enforcement, pilots and citizens. Between July and September, more than 500 sightings were reported, according to FAA data .

articles.title: Mamdani accused of betraying NYC workers as union boss blasts 'anti-labor' horse carriage ban
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani and the City Council aim to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park by 2028, but union leaders say the move betrays workers.
articles.body: New York City lawmakers are set to vote on a bill that would effectively ban all horse-drawn carriages from Central Park — a move that means the tradition dating back to the late 1800s would be taken out to pasture. The City Council is anticipated to approve a bill next week that would abolish the rides — which have been a staple in the Big Apple for more than 150 years — by June 1, 2028. The bill follows an agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin and could mark the first successful effort to ban the rides after previous mayors unsuccessfully pushed to end the industry. "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," a spokesperson for Mamdani’s office said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS Menin, who was the first sitting City Council speaker to support the legislation, also celebrated the decision. "We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing when it's time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city's economic vitality," Menin said. Fox News Digital reached out to Menin for comment but did not immediately receive a response. "Our Administration has been working on a detailed plan for the transition of the workforce and industry, and we have begun discussion of compensation for medallion owners," a City Hall spokesperson said. For years, animal rights advocates have called for an end to Central Park’s horse-drawn carriages, pointing to high-profile incidents involving allegations of animal abuse and the deaths of carriage horses. "New Yorkers are sick and tired of seeing exhausted, sick, lame, elderly horses struggling to pull carriages through Midtown Manhattan, collapsing in the streets," PETA Director of Outreach Communications Ashley Byrne told Fox News Digital. "They've wanted this gone for a long time." Activists have largely denounced the industry as cruel and inhumane, pointing to incidents in which horses have been startled by Manhattan traffic and bolted into oncoming vehicles or onto crowded sidewalks. However, the push to ban the tourist attraction intensified in June. FIREWORKS REPORTEDLY TRIGGER MASS HORSE STAMPEDE THROUGH ROME STREETS, INJURING SEVERAL SOLDIERS On June 17, 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was traveling from India with his family to celebrate his recent graduation, died after being thrown from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park. His death prompted renewed calls for legislation banning horse-drawn carriages. Lawmakers renamed the proposed "Ryder's Law" — named after an elderly horse who collapsed on a Manhattan street in 2022 and later died — "Romanch's Law." "It is tragic and absolutely unforgivable that this industry insisted on dragging this out until countless horses and a teenage human being with his whole life ahead of him died of accidents that never should have happened," Byrne said. The Central Park Conservancy previously reported that the June 17 crash marked the eighth horse-related incident in or around the park in approximately 13 months. Eight days earlier, on June 9, a carriage horse named Deniz collapsed and died while pulling tourists. Fox News Digital reached out to the Mahajan family attorney for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The bill’s new namesake — and the support it has attracted — drew the ire of Alexander Kemp, administrative vice president of the Transit Workers Union (TWU) Local 100, which represents approximately 160 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. LONG ISLAND RAIL ROAD WORKERS GO ON STRIKE, LEAVING 330,000 COMMUTERS WITHOUT SERVICE ON BUSIEST US RAIL LINE "Unfortunately, you had a fatality, a tragedy, with a 18-year-old young man, Romanch," Kemp told Fox News Digital. "And they used it to modify their position. It no longer became about animal welfare, and now this is about an 18-year-old tourist who lost his life tragically in an accident, in a horrific accident." Kemp argued that the City Council used Mahajan’s death to reshape the bill and win over lawmakers after years of unsuccessful attempts to pass a ban. "And they crafted legislation around that, because there was no appetite or evidence to prove that the animals were mistreated and that it was an animal welfare issue. Now they made it a human rights issue. Now they make it a safety issue," Kemp said. Byrne, however, said the issue is rooted in safety concerns, pointing to increased foot traffic and the growing number of wheeled vehicles moving through the park. "Central Park is filled with pedestrians, runners, cyclists, e-bikes and pedicabs," Byrne said. "It is no place for prey animals like horses who can spook at something as slight as a plastic bag blowing through the air or the sound of a car honking." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kemp said many carriage drivers are immigrants nearing retirement age, making it difficult for them to find new jobs if the industry shuts down. "This is what they've done [in their home countries]," Kemp said. "And finding their way in America, this was their golden ticket. This was their street paved with gold. This was an opportunity for them to do something that they've in their country to find a way to feed their family here." Under the legislation, city agencies would have until April 1, 2027, to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers and other industry workers. The plan would also require officials to consider compensation for carriage owners. Additionally, carriage owners would not be permitted to sell their horses for slaughter or for use in other horse-drawn carriage businesses. The animals would have to be rehomed or otherwise placed in a "humane manner." "I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani said at a press conference on Wednesday. Despite the bill’s promises, Kemp argued that Mamdani's administration, which campaigned on a pro-worker platform, is failing to protect the carriage drivers' livelihoods. "If you're going to say to my face that you got labor's back, and then in the middle of the night you take a vote to eliminate a whole industry, well, then that is anti-labor. That is not pro-worker," Kemp said. "So, I don't know how you can satisfy both, just by saying, ‘By the way, that we believe, in our heart, that this industry has come to pasture — no pun intended. And now guys, please, can we hug after we get rid of this industry? Because we have other things we can talk about.’" Kemp also criticized the mayor's administration for promoting pro-immigrant policies while supporting legislation that could eliminate roughly 160 jobs, many held by immigrant workers. "If that is in how you conduct business, and you look at the least of us as the most vulnerable and expendable, then what it tells me is that you are not rooted in the politics of people," Kemp said. "You're rooted in the politics of politics." "And please spare us with all the crocodile tears on how you care about workers and protecting workers and immigrants," he continued. "And just say you're more interested in satisfying the people who give you the most money." The City Council is set to vote on the bill Oct. 22, with supporters expecting it to pass.
