articles.title: Democrats' latest gun-control push runs into inconvenient fact about how school killer was stopped
articles.summary: An armed bystander helped end the deadly Oregon school shooting, but the gun control debate now centers on whether gun-free zones made it worse.
articles.body: Democrats renewed calls for tougher gun laws after three children and a teacher were killed in an Oregon school shooting, but gun-rights advocates say the circumstances of the attack bolster their case against new restrictions. The teenage shooter reportedly opened fire with a shotgun purchased by his mother before an armed father-of-two-students, Kaylub Giamanco, pursued him into Silver Rail Elementary School and fatally shot him. Second Amendment advocates argue additional gun restrictions would not have stopped the killer and could make it harder for armed civilians like Giamanco to intervene. "Democrats are shamefully weaponizing this tragedy in Oregon to advance their political agenda on gun control," Aidan Johnston, director of federal affairs for Gun Owners of America, told Fox News Digital. "But more gun control isn’t the solution. The school was a gun-free zone, and the killer didn’t use a so-called ‘assault weapon.’ What did stop the mass murderer and save lives was an armed bystander with good aim." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS Gun-rights researcher John Lott, president of the Crime Prevention Research Center (CPRC), separately argued that restrictions on carrying guns can leave potential victims defenseless. "These gun-free zones actually serve as a magnet for these attacks rather than stopping them from occurring," Lott told Fox News Digital. Lott pointed to CPRC research examining active shootings from 2014 through 2024, which he said found that legally armed civilians stopped more attacks than police did. The National Rifle Association similarly questioned whether new restrictions would have changed the outcome. "Oregon already has nearly every gun-control measure on the anti-gun wish list — including an A- rating from groups that push them — yet that did not prevent this attack," the NRA said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The armed bystander who pursued the shooter inside and ended the threat is the clearest reminder that, when seconds count, a prepared law-abiding citizen can stop a killer." Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., was among the lawmakers calling for action after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where Bend-LaPine school policy bans firearms, including concealed guns. "The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass commonsense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement. JONATHAN TURLEY: JAMES TALARICO'S DEFENSE OF GUN CONTROL LEAVES OUT A KEY WORD Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., whose district includes Bend, also called for action while acknowledging the armed bystander's intervention. "When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?" Bynum asked during a vigil, after urging action to keep guns away from people who should not have them. Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed, D-R.I., also cited the shooting in calling for additional gun laws and urging the Supreme Court to change course. "It is far past time for the Roberts Court to make it clear their decision on guns does not endorse unfettered and unregulated access to weapons," Reed said. "In the absence of the Supreme Court ceasing its pro-gun rulings, Republicans need to join Democrats in enacting commonsense policies that could prevent these kinds of tragedies." The Roberts court has issued consequential gun-rights rulings, including District of Columbia v. Heller, which struck down the District of Columbia's handgun ban in 2008, and New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn. v. Bruen, which struck down New York's requirement that applicants show a special need to obtain a license to carry a handgun in public. LA GUN OWNERS STUCK WAITING YEARS FOR CONCEALED CARRY PERMITS SCORE MAJOR DOJ VICTORY The political fighting is unfolding as investigators examine how the teenage gunman gained access to his mother's shotgun, a key question in determining whether existing or proposed gun laws could have made a difference. Asked specifically about universal background checks and red-flag laws, the NRA argued that neither would likely have prevented the shooting, citing initial reports that the teenager obtained a family member's firearm. The organization noted that background checks generally apply to firearm transfers, not unauthorized access to a firearm already owned by someone else. It also argued that a red-flag order would likely have been ineffective, although the circumstances surrounding the teenager's access to the shotgun remain unclear. Lott also pointed to a 2021 change in Oregon law that allowed individual school districts to prohibit concealed carry permit holders from bringing guns onto school property, arguing that such restrictions can leave schools more vulnerable. Before that change, Lott said, Oregon teachers with concealed carry permits generally could carry guns at schools, although some districts imposed employment-related restrictions. He estimated that roughly 25 of the state's 197 school districts have adopted prohibitions since then. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "All the school shootings where anybody has been wounded or killed have occurred in places where people, teachers and staff are banned from having guns," Lott said, citing CPRC research. Lott said his organization is updating the research through 2025. He also argued that uniformed school resource officers face tactical disadvantages because attackers can identify them, avoid them or target them first. "Having somebody in uniform is like having a neon sign above them that says, shoot me first," Lott said. Lott also questioned whether penalties for violating gun-free zone restrictions would deter someone already facing multiple life sentences for murder. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They may be facing six or seven life sentences [on murder counts and the like]. Does taking five years away from their seventh or eighth life [sentence] going to matter? Is that a penalty for them? And the answer is no," he said. The NRA also cited research finding that 94% of mass shootings since 1950 occurred in gun-free zones, echoing Lott's argument. "Law-abiding Americans have the right to defend themselves and their communities rather than rely solely on a sign or sticker. The tragedy in Bend is a clear example of how an armed citizen who is prepared and willing to act can stop an attacker and save lives. Policies that keep responsible people disarmed near schools leave those locations more vulnerable, not safer," an NRA spokesperson said. Lott maintained that gun-free zone restrictions can therefore disadvantage lawful gun owners without meaningfully deterring someone planning a mass shooting. Fox News Digital’s James Cirrone and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
articles.summary: The White House is facing growing adversity, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher, weeks before crucial midterm elections.
articles.body:
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.

These were not the best of circumstances.

Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.

The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.

"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."

He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".

In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.

Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis.

And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity.

Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump.

Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash.

A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy.

Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child , proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists.

Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance.

The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving role days after taking job

How did Katie Zacharia do at her first - very brief - White House briefing?

White House defends new press secretary over her legal credentials

Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary

Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate.

And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that.

As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be.

Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary."

Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office.

His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions.

When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues.

In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently.

articles.title: Democratic Senate candidates swamp GOP rivals in fundraising: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Democratic candidates across more than a dozen competitive Senate races raised a combined $253 million from July through September, more than four times the $56 million raised by GOP candidates in those races.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar sift through a new batch of Senate fundraising reports. Plus, Kristen Welker wraps up another week of fiery debates. — Adam Wollner Democratic Senate candidates swamp GOP rivals in fundraising By Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar Democratic candidates across more than a dozen competitive Senate races raised a combined $253 million from July through September, more than four times the $56 million raised by GOP candidates in those races, according to new fundraising reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. During the third quarter, Democratic candidates in these contests spent a combined $300 million, while Republicans spent nearly $84 million. Heading into the final month of the election, Democratic candidates had $87 million on hand compared to $56 million for the Republicans. Republicans were outraised by their Democratic or independent opponents in all but one of the 15 races the NBC News Decision Desk rates as competitive, with Minnesota as the only exception. (Megan Brand has more today on why Republicans think former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya could have an opening there against Democratic Lt. Gov. Penny Flanagan.) Some of the widest gaps came in states where Democrats had long established themselves as prolific fundraisers. In the Texas Senate race, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico raised $60.2 million to state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s $10.2 million. In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff raised $33.1 million while GOP Rep. Mike Collins pulled in $2.8 million. And in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown raised $23.1 million compared to $4.8 million for Republican Sen. John Husted. Democratic candidates’ massive fundraising advantage in some of these states, particularly those that Republicans have won comfortably in recent elections, underscores how the battle for the Senate majority has grown more competitive in the final midterm stretch. It’s also a major reason why Republican outside groups have rushed in to help make up the difference, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the airwaves. Most notably, tech billionaire Elon Musk gave another quarter-billion dollars to GOP groups in recent months. More than half of that money, $158 million, went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership. SLF transferred that same amount to Texas PAC, which has boosted Paxton in Musk’s home state. There are pros and cons of money going directly to candidates’ campaigns versus the outside groups supporting them. Donors are able to give larger amounts to outside groups, which aren’t subject to contribution limits. But candidates are able to get better rates for TV ads and inherently have greater control over how money is spent when it’s in their own accounts. Tensions boil over as the midterms enter crunch time Analysis by Kristen Welker Less than three weeks before Election Day, tensions are boiling over in the heated battle for control of Washington. Just look at what we’ve seen from candidates on the campaign trail this week. Debates have been fiery. Maine Democrat Troy Jackson told Republican Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” after she claimed a protester at their showdown yesterday was a supporter of his. Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan called reports about turmoil in Democrat Mary Peltola’s office indicative of a “character flaw.” And in Georgia’s Senate race, Democratic Sen. John Ossoff asked Republican Rep. Mike Collins if he considers himself a “white nationalist,” while Collins blasted Ossoff over a top Democratic donor appearing in the Epstein files. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are barnstorming the county to rally Republicans and leaning on similar frustrations to motivate Republicans. Both have reserved some of their harshest criticism for Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, whom Vance called a “little weasel” and Trump has called a “jihadist.” It all underscores a key dynamic shaping the closing weeks of the midterms: Trump’s sagging approval rating and voters’ frustration with his handling of the economy is forcing the GOP onto their back heels, giving Democrats the chance to press further into red turf. It’s why we’re seeing Republican groups start to triage House races and cut off incumbents they had hoped could defend their seats, in favor of shoring up more favorable districts. A similar situation has been playing out in the Senate, where money is leaving North Carolina and going into places like Kansas and South Carolina. And it’s why you’re seeing Republicans in battleground races increasingly put distance between themselves and Trump on issues like tariffs and the Iran war on the debate stage and campaign trail. It’s worth emphasizing that the die is not cast. Republicans are playing defense, but they’re doing so in their own territory — and they have hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money at their disposal. But it’s clear that the environment continues to break in Democrats’ direction. And the big question is whether Republicans will be able to keep the bottom from falling out — with an assist from the GOP-leaning map — or if voters’ frustration with the party in power will lead to a widespread rebuke at the ballot box. We’ll discuss all this and more this Sunday on “Meet the Press,” where I’ll speak with Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., who has been barnstorming Southern states in support of Democratic candidates, Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Steve Kornacki will also join us to unveil the results from our latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. articles.title: Katie Zacharia leaves White House role less than a week after starting
articles.summary: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
articles.body:
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.

Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".

Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.

She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.

Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.

"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.

"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.

The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.

As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.

"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.

Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.

After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.

She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".

Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.

When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"

Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"

When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.

She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.

Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"

She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."

Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.

In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.

"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

articles.title: Federal probe of letters containing suspicious substances widens as GOP senators report receiving mailings
articles.summary: A federal investigation of letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to elected officials’ offices has expanded as some Republicans have been identified as targets of the mailings, a person with direct knowledge of the investigation told NBC News on Friday.
articles.body: A federal investigation of letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to elected officials’ offices has expanded as some Republicans have been identified as targets of the mailings, a person with direct knowledge of the investigation told NBC News on Friday. The names of the GOP lawmakers have not been revealed, though they are members of the Senate, the source said. Those lawmakers join a growing list of identified targets including at least 25 state election offices and at least 10 offices of congressional Democrats. Six of those Democrats are senators, including that of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York. On Friday, Reps. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts, Maxwell Frost of Florida, Ritchie Torres of New York and Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey also said offices in their home states received such letters. Democratic Sens. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Alex Padilla of California, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Chris Coons of Delaware and Kirsten Gillibrand of New York have also reported that their offices received suspicious letters. It is not yet clear just how many offices have been targeted by the mailings, though it appears that federal officials are approaching the incidents as being connected. Two other sources familiar with the investigation into the suspicious letters, which contain an unknown white powder substance, said law enforcement has yet to trace the exact origins of the letters or the person or persons responsible for sending them. According to one of the sources, “dozens and dozens” of letters have been sent out nationwide matching the same description. “Everyone is at a loss at the scope of this, and no one knows where this is coming from,” another source told NBC News. “Most of the letters have been addressed to state offices but some to D.C.” The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are leading the investigation. Most if not all the letters sent to the senators were intercepted before they were delivered. One of the sources said preliminary field testing continued through the night on the unknown substance and that so far, all the powder tested has been determined to not be hazardous. Further testing will take place at law enforcement laboratories, the source added. Senate and House staffers received notices on Thursday with warnings about the suspicious packages as officials began to investigate the letters. As of Friday afternoon, state election offices in Alabama, Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming have also received packages. The mailings come less than three weeks before Election Day and after threats against election workers have increased in recent years. Incidents of suspicious substances being mailed to election workers were reported both in 2023 and just weeks before the 2024 presidential election.
